title: A Sugar-Coated Therapy Boosted Brain Cancer Survival by 50% in Mice
hook: An experimental nanoparticle therapy snuck past glioblastoma's toughest defense — the blood-brain barrier — and boosted median survival by 50% in mice, without harming other organs.
key_points: Glioblastoma, an aggressive brain cancer, is hard to treat partly because the blood-brain barrier blocks many therapies from reaching the tumor.
Researchers used sugar-coated nanoparticles to ferry genetic instructions across that barrier and into brain cancer cells.
The nanoparticles restored a key tumor-suppressing protein inside the cancer cells.
In mouse studies, the therapy increased median survival by 50% and shrank tumors, without noticeable damage to other organs.
This is a preclinical, mouse-stage result — not yet tested in people.
content_html: Glioblastoma is one of the toughest cancers to treat partly because the blood-brain barrier — the same defense that protects the brain from toxins — also blocks most therapies from reaching the tumor. A new experimental treatment may have found a way around it.
extra_html: As ScienceDaily reports, researchers used sugar-coated nanoparticles to ferry genetic instructions directly into brain cancer cells, restoring a key tumor-suppressing protein the cancer had lost. In mouse studies, the therapy increased median survival by 50% while shrinking tumors, without noticeable damage to other organs. It's an early, preclinical result — mice aren't people, and glioblastoma has seen promising mouse therapies fail to translate before — but a delivery method that gets past the blood-brain barrier at all is a meaningful piece of the puzzle.

related.hook: A new drug, daraxonrasib, hits a KRAS mutation long thought 'undruggable' and nearly doubled survival in a trial of advanced pancreatic cancer — a hard-to-treat disease.
